 Remember the season when the fish come in?
 DNCT - Every year when October and November come around, my heart yearns for the season when the fish come in and the water rises.
 Báo Đà Nẵng • 08/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 The tranquil river in the countryside, dotted with fishing boats and scenes of people casting nets to make a living in Hoi An Tay ward. Photo: Archival material. My hometown, Que Son, a semi-mountainous region, has always had a harsh climate. In the dry season, the sun is scorching, the fields are parched, and the rice plants wither. In the rainy season, the rains turn the soil muddy, and the village fields are flooded. But for me, the rainy season is a season of memories, of nostalgia...
 The pleasure of listening to heavy-handed speeches.
 Nearly 50 years ago, my village was among the poorest in the country, far from markets and roads, so the traditional staple food was a mixture of fermented soybean paste, pickled vegetables, and fish sauce with added salt, eaten with potatoes, taro, and cassava instead of rice. Therefore, when the rainy season arrived, the addition of fish like tilapia, catfish, frogs, and mole crickets to improve the meal was something everyone looked forward to.
 What I remember most is going to set fish traps. On October afternoons, my mother would be busy in the fields, wearing a straw hat and raincoat, bending over to pull up bundles of rice weeds, the fish getting caught in the weeds, their white bellies exposed. In the evening, she'd come home with a string of fish in her hand, and as soon as she reached the yard, she'd tell me, "The water's rising, let's go set the traps!" So, without eating or drinking, my mother and I would take the string of traps to the field. It was getting dark, the rain was falling heavily on the fields, and I'd part the weeds so my mother could set the traps.
 They say setting fish traps requires skill; some people fill their traps with fish, others come home empty-handed, and some only catch snakes. Setting traps also requires technique; you have to get the opening and the base (in some places, the opening is made at both ends) right, depending on whether the tide is high or low.
 You may also like In September and October, fish from the rivers and streams follow the water up into the rice fields – this is called rising tide fish. By the end of November and December, the tide recedes, and the fish return to the rivers and streams. My mother would dig a small opening in the water to set up the trap, then use a bamboo stick to secure both ends to the bank, holding the trap firmly so it wouldn't drift away. She would then place a clump of grass on top, and that was it. My mother's hands moved swiftly and skillfully in the dim light and amidst the torrential October rain.
 Setting fish traps in the ditch was also a lot of fun. Even now, every time I see the ditch water flowing and the grass growing profusely, I remember, I miss those October nights so much, with my mother and me. Some diligent people would check their traps at midnight to empty them. But I only checked them at dawn. When I put my hand in the trap under the water's surface and felt its weight, and the trap wobbled, oh my god, it was pure bliss. When I lifted it up, it was sure to be a trap full of fish—perch, snakehead, sometimes catfish, tilapia, even eels.
 That's how it is in the countryside; happiness is often so simple. The fish might not fetch much money if you sell them, but the joy of holding the trap and feeling its weight is priceless. It's like setting rabbit traps; the feeling of checking the trap and seeing the line tighten and the fish wriggling is something no amount of money can compare to.
 The mud of my homeland holds onto the scent of love and nostalgia.
 The craft of weaving fish traps is thriving in my hometown. Beautifully woven traps have a soul to them; admiring them is often as captivating as admiring the scenery. The bamboo strips must be evenly shaped, small, and delicate. The weavers must know how to smooth each strip to make it perfectly smooth. Nowadays, there are machines for splitting and smoothing, but in the past, it was all done by hand, the bamboo strips were shaped with a machete, and yet they were all perfectly uniform—truly admirable.
 Then they weave the baskets like baskets, crossing the strips to create perfectly aligned hexagons. Experienced weavers say that a beautiful fish trap should be perfectly round, with a naturally curved tip, and it should appear bright and shiny.
 You may also like In the old days in my hometown of Quế Sơn, the entire Ngô Cang village knew how to weave fish traps, but the most famous and professional in the village was Mr. Ngạt's family, in Quế Châu commune, now Quế Sơn Trung commune, Da Nang . It's said that his family usually had nine people working, each specializing in a different step: shaping the bamboo strips, preparing the frame, weaving, bending the edges, making the trap base, and making the lid... His traps were ordered and transported everywhere, from Chợ Đàng and Đông Phú markets to Việt An and Bà Rén... My hometown has an old folk rhyme: "Đồng Thành has a boar / Phước Đức has a bamboo bucket / Ngô Cang weaves fish traps." 
 From the stories of weaving and setting fish traps to catch fish in the open water, one can see the diligence, resilience, and hard work of the people in this rural area. In the past, they lived faithfully with the fields, ponds, and streams. Now, with a more modern life, the scene of wading through the fields to catch fish, "carrying traps in the middle of the night during storms and rain," has become less common. But no matter how much things change, for the older generation like us, the essence of "the countryside" still lingers in our blood, like a layer of mud, fragrant with the scent of love and nostalgia, clinging to our skin and impossible to wash away.
 In the late afternoons, I go to the fields, sit by the edge of the rice paddies, and watch the harvesting and plowing machines, remembering the buffaloes and harrows of yesteryear. Seeing the persistent rain for days on end brings back memories of setting traps and catching fish in the past. And with a pang of sadness, I remember the image of my mother, a woman who endured hardship and toiled tirelessly across the fields during the fish season when the water level rose.
